The Cobb Hill Gravity Race had three rules. Carts could have no motors, drivers could be pushed only as far as the end of the starting ramp, and every cart had to stop before the hay bales at the bottom. Mira had built hers in the garage over the summer, from a plywood seat, four wheels off an old wagon, and a steering rope tied to the front axle. In practice she had run the hill eleven times. Her best was forty-one seconds.

She steered the way she rode her bicycle, which was constantly. Whenever the cart drifted toward the curb she pulled it back, and whenever it drifted back she pulled the other way, so that she went down Cobb Hill in a long chain of small corrections, like someone carrying a full glass across a room.

On race morning each driver had two runs, and the better one would count. Her first took forty-two seconds. As she dragged the cart back up the sidewalk, the man who sat at the finish with the stopwatch called her over. Everyone knew Mr. Abbott. He had timed the race for as long as anyone could remember, from a lawn chair beside the bales, with a clipboard on his knee.

"Every time you pull that rope," he said, "your wheels scrub sideways. I can hear it from here. Pick your line at the top and leave it alone."

"It drifts," Mira said. "By the bakery it heads for the curb."

"Then let it head for the curb. That street is wide enough for three carts. A foot of drift costs you less than ten pulls on a rope."

At the top, waiting for her second run, she looked down the length of the street and tried to see it the way he must. From the starting ramp the road looked narrow, the curbs close on either side. She had run it a dozen times and had only ever looked at the curbs.

The starter dropped the flag. Mira took the rope in both hands and made herself hold it loosely. Past the church the cart began to slide right, toward the bakery, and every muscle in her arms wanted to pull. She let it slide. The curb came closer, a yard away, then two feet, and stayed there, and the cart ran on, quiet, faster than she had ever felt it go.

Thirty-eight seconds. It was good enough for second place, behind a boy whose cart had ball-bearing wheels and a seat shaped like a bathtub.

Afterward she found Mr. Abbott folding his chair. She wanted to know how many years he had raced, to know one hill that well.

"Never once," he said. "I have watched it, though. Forty years from the bottom of a hill, you learn which drivers are fighting the road."

The man at the lever lets us on last,
my sister and I, and swings the bar down
across our laps with a clank like a gate.
Then the seat lifts, and the fair lets go of us.

Halfway up, the music thins to a tick.
The barker's voice, the bells of the ring toss,
the generator thudding behind the funnel cakes
all fold down into one low hum, like a refrigerator
in another room.

At the very top the wheel stops.
Somebody new is climbing on below,
and we hang there, rocking a little,
higher than the water tower, higher than the steeple,
which from here is only a pencil point.

Everything we know is laid out small:
the feed store with its one green truck,
the school, the ball field with its four white bases
set like sugar cubes on a cloth,
the river turning its shoulder to the town.

My sister finds our street before I do.
She counts the roofs from the corner, three, four,
and there it is, the gray one, the porch light
our mother left on, a single yellow seed.

From the ground our house is the whole world.
From here it is one light among the others,
and I am surprised to find I like it more this way,
small enough to hold up with one thumb,
small enough to keep.

The wheel jerks, and the seat tips forward.
The town slides up behind the striped tents
and is gone, and the hum unfolds into music,
the bells, the barker, the smell of fried dough,

and we come down into the noise
the way you come back into a room
where everyone is still talking,
carrying something none of them saw.

The summer I turned ten, my uncle Wendell took me fishing on the Pine River, and I talked for most of the morning. I had never been fishing before, and I wanted to know everything at once: how deep the water was, whether fish could hear us, what the red-and-white float was for, why he had chosen this bend instead of the one by the bridge, and whether he had ever caught anything bigger than his arm. By my own count, which I kept on my fingers to impress him, I asked thirty-one questions before eight o'clock.

Uncle Wendell answered perhaps four of them. He was my mother's older brother, a tall man who repaired furnaces for a living and who could get through an entire family dinner saying only "please" and "thank you." He showed me how to thread a worm onto the hook so that the point was hidden, and how to cast with a flick of the wrist instead of the whole arm. Then he sat down on an overturned bucket and watched his float.

I watched mine for about a minute. Then I watched a heron on the far bank, and a dragonfly that landed on the tip of my rod, and a boy on the bridge dropping pebbles into the water. Every few minutes I reeled in to check whether the worm was still there, and every time it was, until the last time, when it was gone and the float had been sitting calm the whole while.

"Something took it," I said.

"Something does," said my uncle. It was the longest sentence he had spoken in an hour.

Around ten the sun came over the trees and lay flat on the water, and I ran out of questions. I sat on the bank with my rod across my knees and, for the first time, simply looked at the float. It rode the current in small jerks. It turned, slowly, at the edge of an eddy. Once it dipped and came up, and I felt my uncle go still beside me, and I went still too.

The second dip took it under. I pulled too hard and too late, and the fish, whatever it was, was gone in a swirl of brown water. I waited for my uncle to tell me what I had done wrong. He only baited my hook again, handed the rod back, and nodded once toward the river, as if to say it would still be there.

We caught nothing that day. On the drive home he turned the radio to a ball game and kept it low, and I fell asleep against the window.

It was years before I understood what the morning had been. My uncle had been teaching me the whole time; he simply did it with the river instead of with words. The thirty-one questions were mine. The answers, the ones that mattered, had been floating out there in front of me all along, bobbing in small jerks on the current, waiting for me to stop talking long enough to see them.

At many schools a unit test works like a door that closes behind you. You study, you sit the test on Thursday, and the score goes into the gradebook, where it stays. If you understood the material on Friday instead of Thursday, the gradebook will never know.

The usual defense of this policy is that it teaches responsibility. Adults, the argument goes, get one chance at a job interview or a driving test, and students had better get used to it. But the comparison is weaker than it sounds. A person who fails a driving test is allowed to take it again, usually within a few weeks, and the license that results looks exactly like everyone else's. Most of the tests adults face are built around that second try.

The deeper problem is what a single test is meant to measure. A grade in algebra is supposed to say whether a student can solve equations. A student who could not solve them in October but can in November has learned algebra; the October grade, left standing, reports something that has stopped being true. A school that refuses the retake is, in a small way, choosing an old fact over a current one.

Retakes do have a real cost, and it is worth naming. If every test can be taken again, some students will treat the first attempt as a rehearsal and skip the studying. Teachers who have tried open retakes report exactly this, and their complaint deserves a fair hearing.

The answer is to make the second try earn its place. A student who wants to retake a test might first correct every missed problem on the original and explain, in writing, what went wrong. The work of the retake then happens where learning happens, in the gap between the first attempt and the second, and a student hoping to skip the studying finds that the shortcut is longer than the road.

None of this makes the first test meaningless. It still tells a teacher who needs help, and when. What it should stop doing is deciding, permanently and on one afternoon, how much a student knows. A gradebook ought to record where a student ended up, and a school that keeps a door shut on a student who has since walked through it is grading the wrong day.

item.passage:
In the winter of 1913, the forty-one children of the Fenner Creek School ate their noon meal the way rural children across Carrow County had always eaten it: cold. They carried it from home in tin pails, usually bread and butter, a boiled potato, sometimes a piece of salt pork, and in January the pails sat all morning on a shelf by the door, where the food was often half frozen by noon.

The teacher, a twenty-three-year-old named Ida Larkin, had come from a town school where the children went home for dinner. She noticed that her pupils grew restless and slow in the early afternoon, and that the youngest sometimes put their heads down on their desks and slept. She suspected the cold lunch. She also had, in the middle of the room, a large iron stove that burned all day and heated nothing but the air.

Her plan required almost no money. Each child would bring, along with the usual lunch, a pint jar from home filled with something that could be heated: soup, stewed beans, milk with cocoa, leftover vegetables. At half past ten each morning, two of the older pupils would set the jars in a washtub of water on the stove. By noon the food was hot.

The school board was less sure. One member, a feed merchant named Otis Crane, asked who would pay for the washtub, and another warned that glass jars and a hot stove in a room full of children would end with someone burned. Miss Larkin answered that she had bought the washtub herself for sixty cents, and that the older pupils, who handled hot kettles at home every day, would do the lifting with towels. The board agreed to a trial of one month, on the condition that she report back.

Her report came in March. Attendance on cold days had risen. Fewer children were sent home sick. And Miss Larkin noted something the board had not asked about: the afternoon arithmetic lesson, once the worst hour of her day, had become one of the best.

What changed the board's mind most, however, was the parents. Families who had sent cold potatoes for years began sending soup, and several parents came to the school to see the washtub for themselves. Within two years nine of the county's eleven rural schools were heating jars at mid-morning, and the county superintendent printed Miss Larkin's instructions, down to the hour at which to start the water, in his annual report.

Otis Crane, by then the board's president, liked to tell visitors that the whole program had cost the county exactly nothing. This was true, as far as it went. The washtub on the Fenner Creek stove was still the one Miss Larkin had paid for herself.

Each trap is a single leaf folded into two lobes, hinged along the middle and edged with stiff bristles. On the inner face of each lobe stand a few fine hairs, usually three. These are the trigger hairs, and they are the plant's only way of sensing that something has landed.

Each touch sets off a small electrical signal, and the trap closes only when two signals arrive close enough together. In effect, the plant counts to two.

Researchers who have recorded these signals report that after about five of them the trap seals tightly and begins releasing digestive juices. Charles Darwin, who studied the plant closely, called it one of the most wonderful plants in the world. It is easy to see what he meant.
